analysis.one_liner: Ends tax deductions for corporate fines, penalties, and government settlements.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to stop companies from deducting regulatory fines never got a vote in the Senate Finance Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: When a company pays a fine or a settlement to the government for breaking the law, it can currently write that payment off as a business expense, cutting its tax bill — effectively making taxpayers pick up part of the tab for corporate misconduct. This bill would bar that deduction for amounts paid to the government over violations of law or investigations into them. It would still allow companies to deduct true restitution and payments made to fix the problem, and it would require government agencies to report to the IRS which parts of each settlement are penalties.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who currently absorb part of the cost of corporate fines through the deduction. Law-abiding competitors also gain, because companies that break the law would no longer get a tax break that softens the cost of their penalties. Federal and state governments would collect more tax revenue from violating companies.

how_it_helps.text: The bill denies a tax deduction for any amount paid to a government entity in connection with a violation of law or an investigation into a possible violation, whether paid by suit or settlement.
It preserves deductions only for genuine restitution, payments made to come back into compliance with the law, court-ordered amounts in suits where no government is a party, and taxes actually due.
It even applies the rule to private self-regulatory bodies with enforcement powers in commodities and securities markets, closing a route around the ban.

Government agencies and self-regulatory bodies would have to report to the IRS the penalty, restitution, and compliance components of every settlement of $600 or more, so companies could not quietly re-label penalties as deductible items.

analysis.who_pays: Corporations and financial firms that pay fines, penalties, and government settlements for breaking laws. Their penalties would cost more, because the payment could no longer be deducted against taxable income.

drawbacks.text: Because the restitution and compliance exceptions require amounts to be identified as such in the settlement agreement itself, enforcement agencies would have to structure deals more carefully, and some settlement negotiations could become harder to conclude, which can delay money reaching harmed parties.

The bill applies prospectively but carves out amounts due under binding orders or agreements already entered into, so existing large settlements would keep their deductions until their terms run their course.

Companies facing a stiffer after-tax cost of penalties would have an added reason to fight enforcement in court rather than settle, which can mean slower accountability and higher litigation costs for both sides and the public.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change is straightforward: the public should not help pay for corporate penalties. The restitution and compliance exceptions are well designed, keeping deductible money flowing to actual victims and fixes rather than to the treasury of the violator. The main cost is friction in settlement negotiations and reporting paperwork for agencies, which is modest against the scale of penalty deductions at large financial and industrial firms.

outcome.mechanism: It was read and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Jack Reed introduced the bill with Sen. Chuck Grassley as the cosponsor, giving it one Republican and one Democratic supporter from the start.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance on February 9, 2015; that referral is the last action in the record.
No hearing, markup, or vote on the bill appears in its full action history.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations that deduct fines and government settlements as business expenses kept that tax treatment. Because the bill never moved, the taxpayer cost of that deduction continued unchanged.

for.name: Sen. Jack Reed
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Government Settlement Transparency and Reform Act to deny deductions for corporate regulatory violations.

for.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill on introduction, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action; no markup or vote was ever scheduled in the 114th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had one Democratic sponsor and one Republican cosponsor, and no recorded opposition ever appeared; it simply never reached a vote.

industries.industry: Financial and other corporations that pay government fines and settlements
industries.note: The bill would make fines and settlements fully after-tax costs instead of deductible business expenses, raising the real price of lawbreaking. Banks and large firms facing recurring enforcement actions lose the most.

The bill treats these private enforcers as governmental entities, so their sanctions would become nondeductible and their settlements subject to IRS reporting. The same rule that raises their targets' costs also imposes paperwork on them.
Agencies would have to report the penalty, restitution, and compliance components of settlements to the IRS. This creates administrative work but serves their goal of making penalties meaningful.
